name: journal-paul-and-the-return-that-failed.json
content:
Paul told the church at Thessalonica that he would be alive when Christ returned. He said it was "a word from the Lord". He died, as far as anyone knows, without seeing it, and so did every Thessalonian who heard the promise. The only person in the story who does not appear to have been wrong is the one Paul never met.

The promise in 1 Thessalonians

The Thessalonians had a problem. Some of their number had died, and the survivors feared the dead would miss the return. Paul wrote to settle it: "we do not want you to be uninformed, brothers, about those who are asleep, that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope."1

His answer is precise. "For this we declare to you by a word from the Lord, that we who are alive, who are left until the coming of the Lord, will not precede those who have fallen asleep."2 The Lord will descend "with a cry of command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the sound of the trumpet of God", the dead will rise first, and then "we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air".3

Paul says "we" twice. He includes himself among the living who are left, and he puts the claim under the Lord's authority. The timetable is no guess. He presents it as a message.

[paulus_figure name="old-calendar-pages-7064889"]Old calendar pages. Paul wrote that "the appointed time has grown very short" (1 Corinthians 7:29).[/paulus_figure]

The same expectation elsewhere

The Thessalonian promise is no slip of the pen. To the Corinthians he writes: "Behold! I tell you a mystery. We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet."4 Some of the people he is writing to will still be alive when the trumpet sounds, and he expects to be among them. In the same letter he tells the unmarried to stay as they are because "the appointed time has grown very short".5 [paulus_link slug="was-paul-married" /] shows what that one sentence did to Christian teaching on marriage.

To the Romans he writes: "salvation is nearer to us now than when we first believed. The night is far gone; the day is at hand."6 Three letters, written over perhaps six years, say the same thing in different words. He expected it soon, and he expected to see it.

What he did when it did not come

Later Paul writes differently. In Philippians he weighs death against life: "My desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better."7 The trumpet is gone from the picture. He now expects to die first and be with Christ afterwards. He never says that he had been wrong. He never goes back to the Thessalonians to correct "a word from the Lord" that had not come true. The promise simply stops appearing in his letters. The letter that follows it in the canon, 2 Thessalonians, tells the church not to be shaken by reports that the day has come, and on this site's reading that is the work of Paul's school, written in his name after the fact.

The silence is the offence. A prophet whose forecast fails owes his hearers a correction, and Paul gave none. [paulus_link slug="the-failed-prophet" /] takes this prediction as the test of a prophet, and Paul fails it.

What ʿĪsā said

ʿĪsā gave no timetable. In Mark he says: "concerning that day or that hour, no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father."8 The one the church calls the Son disclaims the knowledge. Paul, who never heard him say it, claims the knowledge and attaches the Lord's name to it. [paulus_link slug="jesus-in-his-own-words" /] sets the two voices side by side on this and on other questions.

The Gospels themselves keep the teacher's admission of ignorance. The apostle's timetable survives only in his letters, and the church has spent two thousand years explaining what he meant.

The delay inside the New Testament

The delay became a crisis within the New Testament. A letter in Peter's name, which many scholars date well after Peter's death, reports that "scoffers will come in the last days", asking: "Where is the promise of his coming? For ever since the fathers fell asleep, all things are continuing as they were from the beginning of creation."9 The people asking had noticed the same thing as this page. The generation Paul spoke of was dying out and nothing had happened.

A Muslim reading

The Qurʾān gives the knowledge of the Hour to God alone (Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:187), and ʿĪsā in the Gospels agrees. A messenger of God does not announce the date of the end and then fail to see it. Paul's timetable belongs with the claims of a man who spoke for himself and used the Lord's name to carry them.

The verdict

Paul promised the Thessalonians, on the authority of the Lord, that he and they would be alive at the return. They were not, and he never admitted it. The teacher he never met had said that not even the Son knew the hour. Paul supplied the hour himself.

A man who invents a timetable and signs it with the Lord's name has told his readers how much to trust the rest of what he reports "from the Lord". The church kept the letters and dropped the promise.

Paul and the return of Christ: questions readers ask

Did Paul expect to see the return of Christ?

Yes. In 1 Thessalonians 4:15–17 and 1 Corinthians 15:51–52 he includes himself among those who will be alive. He writes "we who are alive" and "we shall not all sleep".

Did the return happen in Paul's lifetime?

No source records it. Later letters in the New Testament, such as 2 Peter, show that its delay had become a problem for the church.

Did ʿĪsā give a date for the end?

No. In Mark 13:32 he says that no one knows the day or the hour, "not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father".

Did Paul ever correct the Thessalonians?

No letter shows it. In Philippians he expects to die before the return, but he never withdraws the promise made in 1 Thessalonians.
